title: Saved or die: two wordings
hook: Pick a programme to fight an outbreak, then pick again when it is said in deaths.

knows: what a sure thing and a 1-in-3 chance are
optionally, that losses can feel larger than gains (books:tfs-loss-aversion, a prerequisite only, not re-taught)
doesNotKnow: that "200 will be saved" and "400 will die" out of 600 are the same outcome, so any rule that judges outcomes must answer both wordings the same way

misconception: A sure 200 saved and a sure 400 dead are different offers, so taking the sure thing in one wording and the gamble in the other is consistent.
objective: The learner can explain that the saved and die wordings describe the same outcomes (200 live and 400 die for sure; 1 in 3 all 600 live, 2 in 3 all die), so a rule that judges outcomes picks the sure option in both or the chance in both, and preferring the sure option in one wording and the chance in the other fits no such rule.

claims.text: The stage's options and their bars (600 cells each, filled = alive; stage key '■ = alive · □ = die'): saved wording '200 people will be saved' (200 live, 400 die, for sure) and 'a 1-in-3 chance all 600 are saved, a 2-in-3 chance nobody is'; die wording '400 people will die' (the same outcome as the first) and 'a 1-in-3 chance nobody dies, a 2-in-3 chance all 600 die' (the same as the second). With the toggle 'Say both in the same words' on, the die options read '200 people will be saved' and 'a 1-in-3 chance all 600 are saved, a 2-in-3 chance nobody is' in place. Reveal, every branch: 'In the same words, 400 sure to die is 200 sure to be saved, and the two chances are one chance.'

claims.text: Any rule that ranks options by their outcomes and strictly prefers one option to the other picks the sure option in both wordings or the chance in both (C has A's outcomes and D has B's), so someone who prefers the sure 200 saved, then the 1-in-3 chance nobody dies, fits no such model: predict 'Someone prefers the sure 200 saved, then, in the 'die' wording, the 1-in-3 chance nobody dies. Can one model that judges outcomes fit both?', answer 'No: same programmes, two wordings'. Only a rule that ranks the two as a toss-up (expected value, 200 = 200) fits a mixed pair, and it is excluded by 'prefers'. A sure-sure or chance-chance pair fits some strict rule, so 'No: only the sure option both times fits' is false.
claims.source: Brief 4 claim (2) and Decisions (r4) 1-2; node company/domains/briefs/checks/behavioral-gain-loss-framing.mjs checks '(a) every outcome-based rule tried' (31 rules), '(a) mixed pairs fit only rules that rank the two programmes as a toss-up', '(a) both matched pairs fit some strict rule' and 'predict answer follows from the derivation'. Builder statement, not self-verified.
claims.note: FC pass 63 (fact-checker, 2026-10-16, SO-10-2, server 6838dbac :3591): VERIFIED (the FC pass 57 dispute is resolved). Own node, 312 outcome-only rules (u = x^a, a = 0.01-3.00; exponential utility; TK probability weighting with u = x; worst; best): A-vs-B equals C-vs-D for every rule; no strict rule fits A+D or B+C; the only tie is u = x^1 (EV 200 = 200); A+C fits a strict rule (x^0.5) and B+D fits one (x^2, best case), so option 2 is false. Predict on :3591 says 'prefers' and answer 'No: same programmes, two wordings'. Note: '(expected value, 200 = 200)' is an example of a toss-up rule, not the only possible one; the claim's 'only a rule that ranks the two as a toss-up' is what is true. claims.note: FC pass 63 (fact-checker, 2026-10-16, SO-10-2, server 6838dbac :3591): VERIFIED. All three names render in their branches as quoted. Source opened first-hand this pass (PMC OAI-PMH, PMC8432807, Rachev et al. 2021): 'In the risky-choice framing effect, different wording of the same options leads to predictably different choices' and 'people tend to be risk-averse when presented with potential gains but tend to be risk-seeking when the same options are presented as potential losses'. So A-then-D is the named pattern and B-then-C its reverse. 'Would fit none' holds under the strict 'Preferring' (c2). claims.text: Recall: 'Someone prefers to take a treatment described as '90% survive', and to refuse it described as '10% die'. Can one model that judges outcomes fit both?' Answer 'No: same outcome, two descriptions': '90% survive' and '10% die' describe the same outcome (900 of 1,000 live in both), so a model that judges outcomes can take it both times or refuse it both times, but cannot prefer to take it one way and refuse it the other; 'No: only taking it both times fits' is false because refusing both times also fits.
claims.source: 1,000 × 0.9 = 1,000 − 1,000 × 0.1 = 900 (node company/domains/briefs/checks/behavioral-gain-loss-framing.mjs, recall checks; brief 4 transfer recall, reworked r4). Builder statement, not self-verified.
claims.note: FC pass 63 (fact-checker, 2026-10-16, SO-10-2, server 6838dbac :3591): VERIFIED. meta.json recall.why equals the brief-4 script's recallWhy (fcd3e95, written by cm-behavioral) character for character, and equals the meta.json at server 6838dbac; question and options match the script too. Own node: 90% survive of 1,000 = 900 live; 10% die of 1,000 = 100 die, 900 live, so the same outcome. 'Cannot prefer to take it one way and refuse it the other' is true under strict preference; taking and refusing both times each fit some outcome model, so option 2 is false. Answer index 2. recall.question: Someone prefers to take a treatment described as '90% survive', and to refuse it described as '10% die'. Can one model that judges outcomes fit both?
options: Yes: '10% die' is the worse offer
No: only taking it both times fits
recall.why: Out of 1,000 patients, 900 live and 100 die under both descriptions. A model that judges outcomes can take it both times or refuse it both times, but cannot prefer to take it one way and refuse it the other.
